title: 3rd Stopping Place 4th Truth Lawful Provision Comes Through Weakness And Trust In Allah

questions.question: What example from nature shows that some living things receive food without moving to get it?
questions.answer: Trees stay where they are, and their nourishment comes to them.

questions.question: How does the passage describe the feeding of babies in their earliest stage?
questions.answer: Their milk reaches them through amazing small means, together with the care and mercy shown by their mothers.

questions.question: What change happens when babies gain some ability and choice?
questions.answer: Their milk stops.

questions.question: According to the passage, what does the tree-and-infant example prove about lawful provision?
questions.answer: It shows that lawful provision does not come mainly because of strength or personal control, but because of weakness, need, and trusting in Allah.

questions.question: What harmful trait can come from having will, strength, and cleverness?
questions.answer: They can lead a person to greed.

questions.question: What bad result of greed is mentioned for some educated people?
questions.answer: It can push them into a needy, dependent life.

questions.question: What surprising result is mentioned for a simple and ordinary person who relies on Allah?
questions.answer: Such a person may end up with wealth.

questions.question: What is the main lesson of the proverb about the scholar and the ignorant person?
questions.answer: Earning lawful provision is not simply the result of intelligence or effort; it comes through mercy, while effort is only accepted as a means.

questions.question: Which kind of provision is guaranteed?
questions.answer: The real and natural kind that life truly needs.

questions.question: How does the passage use body fat and similar reserves as evidence?
questions.answer: It says the body stores enough nourishment to help a person survive for many days even without eating.

questions.question: According to the passage, why do some people seem to die of hunger before those stored reserves are used up?
questions.answer: The passage says it is really due to illness caused by carelessness and the shock of broken habit, not a true lack of provision.

questions.question: Why do trees serve as an important example in this passage?
questions.answer: They need sustenance but cannot choose or struggle for it, yet they still receive it.

questions.question: What attitude is connected with the way trees receive sustenance?
questions.answer: Reliance on Allah.

questions.question: What does the early feeding of infants suggest about who provides for the weak?
questions.answer: It suggests that Allah provides for those who are helpless.

questions.question: Why is the stopping of milk after a baby grows stronger important to the argument?
questions.answer: It supports the idea that provision is especially sent in a special way during times of weakness and need.

questions.question: In this passage, what is the relationship between greed and human abilities?
questions.answer: Strong will, power, and skill can stir up greed.

questions.question: What contrast does the passage make between some learned people and some ordinary people?
questions.answer: Some learned people struggle and still face poverty, while some simple people who rely on Allah may receive wealth.

questions.question: What does this contrast teach about the source of lawful provision?
questions.answer: It teaches that its source is divine mercy, not merely human talent or planning.

questions.question: How is human effort treated in the passage?
questions.answer: Effort matters as something accepted, but it is not the real creator of provision.

questions.question: What makes the first type of provision “true and natural”?
questions.answer: It is the kind actually needed to keep a living being alive.

questions.question: What does the passage say the Sustainer guarantees?
questions.answer: The necessities of life.

questions.question: How does the passage argue that the body is prepared for times without food?
questions.answer: It says the body holds reserves, like fat, that can keep a person going for a while.

questions.question: What deeper point is being made by the discussion of bodily reserves?
questions.answer: It shows planning, order, and mercy in how living beings are sustained.

questions.question: What does the passage say trees lack, even though they still receive sustenance?
questions.answer: They lack power and will.

questions.question: What does the word “trusting” mean in the example of trees?
questions.answer: It means depending on Allah instead of relying on one’s own ability.

questions.question: What two things help the baby receive nourishment in the passage?
questions.answer: The special way milk is delivered and the loving care of the mother.

questions.question: What conclusion does the passage draw from the cases of trees and infants?
questions.answer: Weakness and need are closely connected to receiving lawful sustenance.

questions.question: Why are strength and cleverness not praised without limits in this section?
questions.answer: Because they can feed greed and lead to loss.

questions.question: What does the passage suggest about worldly success and education?
questions.answer: Education alone does not guarantee provision.

questions.question: What role does mercy play in receiving lawful sustenance?
questions.answer: Mercy is presented as the real source that grants it.

questions.question: What role does striving play in receiving lawful sustenance?
questions.answer: Striving is a proper means that is accepted, but it does not force provision to happen.

questions.question: How many main categories of sustenance are introduced in this passage section?
questions.answer: Two.

questions.question: What evidence from the human body supports the claim that basic provision is guaranteed?
questions.answer: The body stores nourishment inside itself for many days.

questions.question: If someone dies before those reserves should be gone, what explanation does the passage give?
questions.answer: The cause is described as sickness linked to carelessness and disturbed habits, not simple starvation.

questions.question: What pattern do trees and young babies share in this passage?
questions.answer: Both are weak in getting food for themselves, yet their sustenance reaches them.

questions.question: What lesson about Allah’s care can be learned from that pattern?
questions.answer: Allah’s provision especially appears in the case of the weak and needy.

questions.question: Why is the ending of milk after a child gains some ability meaningful?
questions.answer: It shows that the earlier special nourishment matched the child’s helpless stage.

questions.question: What does the passage connect with loss and harm in seeking provision?
questions.answer: Greed.

questions.question: According to the passage, can intelligence by itself secure lawful provision?
questions.answer: No; intelligence by itself does not guarantee it.

questions.question: How does the proverb support the argument of the passage?
questions.answer: It gives a familiar example showing that effort and knowledge do not always bring wealth, while others receive provision more easily.

questions.question: What does the passage identify as the real giver of lawful sustenance?
questions.answer: Divine mercy joined with compassion for need.

questions.question: How should we understand human work in light of this teaching?
questions.answer: Work is a proper part of life, but the final giving of provision belongs to Allah.

questions.question: What is meant by “true and natural” provision?
questions.answer: It means the basic nourishment required to stay alive.

questions.question: What does the guarantee of this basic provision say about Allah’s care for creation?
questions.answer: It shows steady care and planning for living beings.

questions.question: How does the passage use the number of days a body can survive without food?
questions.answer: It uses that fact to argue that Allah has already placed provision within the body.

questions.question: What mistaken conclusion does the passage try to correct about early death from hunger?
questions.answer: It corrects the idea that such a death always comes from no provision at all; instead, it may come from illness caused by poor caution and broken routine.

questions.question: In the passage, what happens to the food needed by trees?
questions.answer: It comes to them while they remain where they are.

questions.question: What human example is placed beside trees to strengthen the same point?
questions.answer: Very young children being fed with milk.

questions.question: Why does the passage mention a mother’s tenderness?
questions.answer: To show one of the merciful ways provision reaches helpless babies.

questions.question: What principle about lawful sustenance is stated after these examples?
questions.answer: It is not measured mainly by a creature’s strength or choice.

questions.question: What inner attitude is linked to weakness and need in this section?
questions.answer: Trust in Allah.

questions.question: What danger can come when people depend too much on their own skill and power?
questions.answer: They may become greedy and suffer loss.

questions.question: What social comparison is made to prove this point?
questions.answer: Some highly educated people end up struggling, while some rough and simple people receive wealth.

questions.question: According to the passage, what does this comparison reveal about the way provision is given?
questions.answer: It reveals that lawful provision comes from mercy and compassion, not just from human ability.

questions.question: What are we told about the first kind of sustenance?
questions.answer: It is the genuine kind needed for life and it is guaranteed.

questions.question: What sign of order is found in the way this first kind is given?
questions.answer: The body itself keeps stored nourishment ready for hard times.

questions.question: About how long does the passage say these stored reserves can support life?
questions.answer: At least around twenty days.

questions.question: If a person dies sooner than that without food, what reason does the passage give?
questions.answer: It says the death comes from sickness caused by lack of care and the upsetting of normal habits.

questions.question: What does the passage teach through the example of a tree standing still while receiving sustenance?
questions.answer: It teaches that provision can come from Allah even without a creature’s own effort or movement.

questions.question: How does the example of infants deepen that lesson?
questions.answer: It shows that the weakest humans are given nourishment in a very caring and direct way.

questions.question: Why is the stopping of milk later on an important detail?
questions.answer: It marks a shift showing that special provision was tied to the infant’s helplessness.

questions.question: What does the passage say lawful sustenance is connected to more than strength and will?
questions.answer: It is connected to weakness, need, and reliance on Allah.

questions.question: What bad character trait may grow out of strong will and cleverness?
questions.answer: Greed.

questions.question: How can greed affect even knowledgeable people?
questions.answer: It can leave them in a needy condition despite their learning.

questions.question: What message is carried by the saying about the struggling scholar and the provided-for ignorant person?
questions.answer: Learning and planning do not control provision; Allah gives it through mercy.

questions.question: Does the passage reject working and striving altogether? Explain.
questions.answer: No. It says working and striving are accepted, but they are not the true source of provision.

questions.question: What division of sustenance is introduced next?
questions.answer: The passage divides sustenance into two types.

questions.question: How is the first type defined?
questions.answer: It is the real, natural nourishment needed to preserve life.

questions.question: What proof is offered that this first type is guaranteed?
questions.answer: The body contains stored food reserves, such as fat, that support life when food is not available.

questions.question: What explanation does the passage give for some deaths that seem to come from hunger too quickly?
questions.answer: It explains them as caused by sickness connected to carelessness and disrupted habits rather than by the complete absence of provision.
